keywords: how to set up an altar
lede: A ritual that goes wrong usually goes wrong at the joins. The intention was fine, the flame was fine, and the working still collapsed because the room was not cleared, the end was not marked, or nobody wrote down what had happened. The fix is not a better technique. It is an order of operations that treats the unglamorous parts as mandatory. What follows is one complete working written as a sequence, from the sentence you start with to the line you write in the log afterwards, with the materials named and the reasoning given at each step. It assumes you have almost nothing and intend to acquire things slowly. There is a section on substituting materials, because a working that breaks when you cannot find one particular item was never really a working. And there is a step most people skip entirely, which is deciding in advance what would count as a result, because without that the review afterwards becomes a negotiation rather than a measurement.

sections.h2: Step one, write the work down in a single imperative
p: Before any object is touched, write one sentence in the imperative mood. Not a description of what you want, which is a wish, and not a question, which is divination. An instruction to yourself or to a situation, in the form you would give it to a colleague. The sentence should name one thing and one measurable condition, because a sentence containing four aims cannot be evaluated later and will therefore be judged by whether you happen to like how you feel.

Write it where you will see it again. The most common error at this stage is producing a beautiful statement of aspiration and never showing it to anybody, including yourself. This is a working document, not a declaration, and its only job is to be checked against reality at the end of the window you set in the next step.

sections.h2: Step two, choose the materials you will actually use
p: Pick the objects and then commit to them for this working. The failure mode here is a kit spread across a table where nothing has a clear role, which produces a working with no focal point and a cleanup that takes longer than the ritual. One surface, one implement for making the mark, one vessel, one flame source, and one item that is purely for clearing. Five things, each with a named job, is more than adequate for almost any work you would attempt this year.

If you are working with correspondence, choose the correspondence before you choose the objects, so that the objects follow the specification rather than dictating it. A colour chosen because it was already in the drawer is not a correspondence. It is an accident that will look like a decision in the log six weeks later.

sections.h2: Step three, prepare the space before you sit down
p: Clear the surface completely, including the ordinary clutter that accumulates on a table over a week. Physical disorder in the working area produces a specific and well-documented kind of difficulty: attention fragments toward the unresolved items and the working becomes a series of short disconnected attempts rather than one sustained sequence. This is a cognitive effect, not a spiritual one, and it is one of the few places where tidying genuinely changes the outcome.

Open a window if you will be burning anything. Turn off notifications on any device you are using. Decide what time you will stop, and write that time down as well, because a working with no declared end is a working that will be abandoned the moment something more convenient arrives.

sections.h2: Step four, set the timing and decide what would count
p: Two decisions here, and the second one is the one that changes everything downstream. First, the window: a date by which you will review, written before the working rather than after. Thirty days is a reasonable default for something you can observe. Second, and more important, the observation you will make. If the sentence asks for a reply from a particular person, the observation is that reply. If it asks for a change in your own routine, the observation is a count in your log, not a feeling you had on a good day.

Write both down in the same hand as the intent. The purpose is not bureaucracy. It is to remove the opportunity for reinterpretation at the review stage, when you will be strongly motivated to find evidence that the working succeeded because you invested in it. Pre-committing to a specific observation is the single most effective protection against that motivation.

sections.h2: Step five, the scent, chosen rather than tolerated
p: If you are using incense, choose it deliberately and use less than you think. A working room should be recognisably scented to someone who walks in blind, and should not have been difficult to sit in for twenty minutes. Excessive smoke makes concentration harder rather than easier, which is the opposite of what the atmosphere is supposed to be for. If your material is overpowering at the amount the tradition suggests, that is information about the tradition, not about your tolerance.

You can also run the entire working with no scent at all, and the record will not show a difference worth reporting. Scent is a genuine anchor across sessions, so it is worth using if you intend to work repeatedly, and entirely optional for a one-off. The mistake is assuming it carries part of the effect, which makes its absence feel like a failure when nothing is actually missing.

sections.h2: Step six, the charge, kept short on purpose
p: Whatever your tradition prescribes, compress it. The instructions that describe half an hour of repetition are describing a state of attention rather than a quantity of work, and a state of attention is fully available in about ninety seconds. Practise the short version until the long version becomes a way of avoiding the short one. A working that takes twenty minutes and could have taken two is a working that will not be repeated on a bad day.

The single most common error at this step is the addition of improvisation. If you find yourself adding gestures because the sequence feels thin, stop and write down what you are adding. Usually it is filler, and it is usually filling space that should be occupied by repetition of the sentence you wrote in the first step.

sections.h2: Step seven, the ending, made unambiguous
p: Close it in a way that cannot be confused with continuing later. Put the flame out, close the notebook, put the object somewhere you will not touch it again, and leave the room. The tradition of dismissal exists for a good structural reason: an unfinished ritual occupies attention in the background, and a working you keep returning to mentally is a working that never actually closed.

This step takes about fifteen seconds and it is the step most often abandoned. People get to the end of a working feeling tired, decide the clearing is optional, and go to bed with the room still arranged. Nothing dramatic follows, but the next session starts from a cluttered surface and an unfinished prior sequence, and the whole apparatus degrades a little at a time.

sections.h2: Step eight, the record, written before you stand up
p: One line, in the same session, while the sequence is still in mind. Date, the sentence, the materials, the declared end time, and the observation you will make at the review. That is the whole entry and it takes about forty seconds. The reason it must happen in the session is that memory reorders, and a note written a day later will quietly include whatever you have since decided the working meant.

Add a second line, if you have the energy, on how the working actually felt while you were doing it. That field turns out to be the most diagnostic one in the log over time, because it captures the variable that the other fields cannot, which is whether you were actually present. Every other column is objective, and presence is the thing that varies most between sessions.

sections.h2: A complete sequence you can copy
p: Here is the whole working in order, using nothing beyond paper, a pen, a dish, a cloth and matches. The whole thing occupies about twenty-five minutes including the setup, and you could run it tomorrow evening without acquiring anything at all. The structure is deliberately rigid so that the variable under examination is you, rather than the arrangement.
ol: Write the intent as one imperative sentence, on a fresh page.
Write the review date and the observation beside it.
Clear the surface completely and open the window.
Reduce the sentence to a glyph and draw it once, without redrawing.
Light a match, hold the page in the flame, close it, put it out.
Clear the space, leave the room, and log one line before returning.

sections.h2: Working with a room that will not cooperate
p: Sometimes the space is wrong. A shared flat, a partner asleep, a room that doubles as an office, a building where someone will walk in at any moment. There are two honest responses and one dishonest one. The dishonest response is to work anyway while worrying about interruption, which produces a working you will remember as compromised regardless of what else happened.

The honest responses are to move the working to a time the space is reliably available, or to reduce it to a form that can be performed standing up in ninety seconds. The short form is worth practising anyway, because a method you can do anywhere is a method you will actually do on the days when the conditions are poor, and those days are most of the useful ones.

sections.h2: Which substitutions are safe and which are not
p: Almost every object in a working can be substituted, because the objects are standing in for qualities and the qualities can be carried by other things. A different vessel, a different pen, a different candle, a different room, a different hour. These substitutions cost you very little and the record will not show the difference. What cannot be substituted is the structure: the stated intent, the reduction, the single charge, the unambiguous ending and the written observation. Those five are the working.

The one substitution to be careful with is the clock. If a tradition specifies a duration, and you substitute a different one, record the substitution. Durations are usually arbitrary and the substitution is rarely the reason a working does nothing, but a log that quietly alters the specification cannot answer any question you later want to ask of it.

sections.h2: When a missing object is the real obstacle
p: There is a version of this problem where the absence of an object genuinely blocks you, and it is worth recognising so you can stop treating it as a discipline problem. It occurs when you have attached a real expectation to a particular item, usually one you have seen described rather than used. The expectation is doing the work, not the item, and the block will persist until you either acquire the item and find it changes nothing, or notice what the item stood for.

If a missing object is blocking you, write down what you believe it will do. Most of the time the answer is some version of making the work feel finished, and you can achieve that by writing the date at the top of the page and closing the notebook properly. The object was a way of marking a boundary, and the boundary can be marked without it.

sections.h2: Turning a flaw in the setup into part of the design
p: A surprising number of working methods work better when something about them is awkward. The room is not private, so the working has to be brief and the conclusion has to be immediate, and both of those are good design. You have no incense, so there is no scent cue, and you find you remember the workings by where in the evening they happened instead, which is arguably a better anchor than a fragrance.

Treat an awkward condition as information about the design rather than as an excuse to postpone. Ask what constraint is being imposed, and then ask whether the same constraint would be worth choosing voluntarily. Often the answer is yes, because the constraint is doing the work that you would otherwise have filled with apparatus. This is the most useful thing about a limited kit: it forces the method to be explicit about which parts are carrying it.

sections.h2: The ten-minute version for days you have no evening
p: A compressed working, for the evenings when a full sequence will not happen. No clearing, no scent, no vessel, no standing. Sit down, write the sentence, reduce it, draw it once, hold your fingertip on the page for a count of fifty, close the notebook, and log one line. Six minutes, once you have written the routine down to the point where it runs itself.

This version is where most of the value in a long practice is actually collected, because it is the version you will perform on a bad evening, and frequency is the variable that separates a method from a memory. If your practice has quietly become the full twenty-five minute version only, it has also quietly become a practice that stopped six months ago.

faq: What does the free version of this leave me unable to do?

Very little, and it is worth being specific rather than reassuring. Free material will not give you a correspondence table you can query, a lunar or planetary calculation, or a reliable astrological reference, so the specification part of a working takes longer to assemble. Everything that actually constitutes the method, which is the statement, the reduction, the charge, the ending and the record, is available at no cost and has been for as long as the tradition itself.
How long should the charge last before I stop?

Long enough to be unmistakably intentional and short enough that you stay awake for all of it. Ninety seconds of sustained repetition of the sentence is more than enough for most purposes, and the traditions that prescribe half an hour are describing attention rather than duration. If you cannot stay present for the time your tradition specifies, shorten the time rather than abandoning the working, and record the change.
Do correspondences matter at this stage?

Not yet, in most cases. Correspondences are worth learning once the basic sequence runs without your attention, because until then any extra layer is something you will drop under mild pressure and then blame the working for failing. Get the five structural elements in place for a month first. The correspondence will still be there afterwards, and it will be much easier to apply once you are not using attention to remember the sequence.
Should I do this daily or only on a chosen day?

Daily, at the compressed length, with the full version reserved for a chosen day once a week. The reason is that the association is built by frequency and the log is built by discipline, and the compressed version is the only one of the two that survives contact with an ordinary week. If you only ever work on a chosen day, you will produce about one entry a month, which is not enough data to tell you whether any of this is doing anything.
Does software make the ritual sequence clearer or just busier?

Not for the method itself, though several do one component of the bookkeeping well. A timer enforces the short charge more reliably than intention will. A lunar reference removes an avoidable error. An archive that timestamps your entries removes the temptation to rewrite yesterday, which is the one place where a tool genuinely adds integrity. That last category is the one worth paying for if anything is.
